risk_of_bias.note: The only evidence on passing urine is one case report (card sc_bryden_1995: JBI checklist, high risk for any statement about cause): the drug was never identified in the man or the tablets, the amount is his own account given in two stages, no bladder measurement or follow-up is reported, and no other cause was excluded beyond a normal examination. The hormone evidence comes from a before-and-after study with 3 untreated comparison occasions that were not compared statistically and one-tailed tests at one time point (card sc_henry_1998: ROBINS-I serious) and from a placebo-controlled study that collected urine and reported no urine result, was not registered and prints degrees of freedom that do not match the analyses described (card sc_baggott_2016: RoB 2 high).

inconsistency.note: No two studies measured passing urine, so there is nothing to be inconsistent on the claim's outcome. On the hormone, the uncontrolled study found a rise and the placebo-controlled studies found none (vasopressin and copeptin in Baggott et al., 2016; copeptin in Hysek et al., 2014); the statement reports both, and since the hormone is not the claim's outcome this is counted under indirectness, not again here.

indirectness.note: The controlled studies measured the hormone, copeptin and blood sodium, not difficulty passing urine, urine volume or bladder function, and none tested whether the hormone has anything to do with difficulty passing urine; they were done in healthy volunteers given one known dose by researchers. The case concerns one man and tablets of unknown content.

imprecision.note: One case; laboratory samples of 8, 16, 12 and 32 people, the water-load comparison resting on the 10 people with usable data from both sessions; no interval is printed for any hormone or sodium result, and the sodium sizes are read from figures.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. A single case is published because it is unusual, which the statement respects by giving no frequency; the urine collected and not reported in Baggott et al. (2016) is rated under risk of bias.

rate.reasoning: The only evidence on the claim's outcome, difficulty passing urine, is one case report: observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness (the controlled studies measured a hormone and blood sodium, not passing urine) and one for imprecision; very low (the floor). Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study read measured how often passing urine becomes difficult after MDMA, or why. The placebo-controlled studies (Baggott et al., 2016; Hysek et al., 2014) would start high for their own outcomes, but they do not measure this claim's outcome and so do not raise it; their finding of no rise in the hormone or copeptin disagrees with the uncontrolled rise in 8 men (Henry et al., 1998), and the statement reports both without choosing an explanation. The alpha-adrenergic account is the case authors' reasoning, and no study read tested the hormone against urine; neither account is asserted. Status: single study (one case report on passing urine). Amounts appear only as each study's conditions, and the claim gives no advice on amounts or fluid.
rate.population: People who take MDMA: one healthy 19-year-old man treated by a hospital urology team in the UK (case report); in laboratory studies, 8 healthy men aged 22 to 32 in London (Henry et al., 1998), 16 people (8 women, 8 men; aged 18 to 42) and 12 people (6 women, 6 men; aged 21 to 40) in the USA, all healthy and with earlier MDMA use (Baggott et al., 2016), and 32 healthy volunteers in Basel (16 women, 16 men; aged 20 to 31; 22 had never taken MDMA) (Hysek et al., 2014)
rate.exposure: MDMA: in the case, tablets sold as ecstasy, 15 in the 36 hours before admission by the man's own account, content untested (as reported, not a recommendation); in the laboratory, a single oral dose given by researchers (study conditions): 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL of water (Henry), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride with drinking limited to about 473 mL an hour or followed an hour later by 20 mL/kg of water drunk within 30 minutes (Baggott), or 125 mg (Hysek)
rate.comparator: None in the case report; each man's own values before the dose, and 3 of the men on a later untreated occasion, not compared statistically (Henry); placebo in the same people on another day, double-blind (Baggott, Hysek), with prazosin as a check drug in Baggott's first study and the same water load after placebo in the second
rate.outcome: Difficulty passing urine, urine volume and bladder function (not measured or not reported in any study read; one case of acute retention of urine described); antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and copeptin; blood sodium
rate.magnitude: Bryden et al. (1995), one case: man aged 19; acute retention for 24 hours before referral; painful palpable bladder; examination and urinalysis otherwise normal; urethral catheter removed after 36 hours on free drainage; no further retention (follow-up length not stated); self-reported use: only ecstasy in the previous 12 months, one or two tablets once or twice a week, then 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission (earlier amphetamine and cannabis); no drug screen, no tablet analysis, no residual volume, flow study or imaging. Henry et al. (1998), 8 healthy men aged 22-32, 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL water at 10:00: vasopressin range 1.14-1.88 pmol/L before and 2.46-9.16 at 2 hours (paired t test, one-tailed p = 0.006; about 0.012 two-tailed, editors' calculation), maximum between 1 and 2 hours, against a small decrease on 3 later untreated occasions (not compared statistically); sodium 139-145 mmol/L before and 140-142 at 2 hours, down 1-3 in 7 of 8 and up 1 in one (one-tailed p = 0.025; about 0.05 two-tailed, editors' calculation); urine not measured. Baggott et al. (2016), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride (1.26 mg/kg base) or placebo, double-blind, within person, sequence- and gender-balanced: Study 1 (16 people, 8 women; water limited to about 473 mL an hour; 1213 +/- 76 mL drunk in 8 hours, not differing by condition): maximum ADH by condition F(3,45) = 5.68, p = 0.002; prazosin alone z = 3.46 (p = 0.002), prazosin with MDMA z = 3.22 (p = 0.004), MDMA alone z = 1.21 (p = 0.589); minimum sodium by condition F(3,357) = 8.44 (p < 0.0001), MDMA alone t(357) = -4.05 (p < 0.0001), MDMA with prazosin t(357) = -3.50 (p = 0.0005), prazosin alone no effect; MDMA curves under 2 mmol/L below placebo at their lowest, around 3 hours (editors' approximate reading of Figure 3a). Study 2 (12 people, 6 women; 20 mL/kg water within 30 minutes, an hour after the capsule; two people who vomited in their MDMA sessions excluded): maximum ADH F(1,15) = 0.113 (p = 0.74), maximum copeptin F(1,9) = 0.019 (p = 0.89); minimum sodium F(1,9) = 13.2 (p = 0.005); means about 133.6 mmol/L at 3 hours after MDMA against about 137.7 after placebo, whose lowest mean was about 136 at 2 hours (editors' approximate readings of Figure 3b); one woman 127 mmol/L at 3 hours, transient, without symptoms. No mean, change or interval is printed for any sodium result. Urine pooled before dosing and over 0-8 and 8-24 hours; no urine result reported. Hysek et al. (2014), 32 healthy volunteers (16 women), 125 mg against placebo, double-blind crossover: copeptin before and 1 and 2 hours after not altered (no statistic printed). No study gives a frequency of difficulty passing urine.
rate.short: Nobody knows: no study has measured it. A water-holding hormone rose in 8 men on MDMA. Three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker.
rate.rate: One case report with no drug test, plus lab studies that measured a hormone and blood salt but not peeing. And their hormone results disagree.

risk_of_bias.note: Poison-centre reports: the drug is the caller's report as coded, never confirmed in a laboratory; voluntary reporting favours people with symptoms; half of all reports (those with other substances) were excluded; codes changed in 2016; two percentages in the text contradict the table (card sc_carpenter_2019: JBI, moderate as a description, high as evidence of what a named drug does). Published cases: severe and detected cases, chosen by one author with no stated rule for judging contribution, not appraised, with some people apparently listed twice (card sc_brunetti_2021: high).

inconsistency.note: The two sources agree in direction: the reported effects are mostly sedation, and deaths without other drugs are rare in both (1 death among 234 single-substance poison-centre reports; 3 of 141 death entries in the review's table list no other drug).

indirectness.note: The deaths are known only through a review's compilation of case reports, which were not read (second-hand); the poison-centre data cover single-substance reports only, while most deaths involved other drugs; neither source compares designer with prescribed benzodiazepines, which is why the claim is worded as insufficient evidence for that comparison.

imprecision.note: Counts of reports; the one death among 234 single-substance reports is a single event, which the statement gives as a count.

publication_bias.note: The selection of published cases is counted under risk of bias, not twice.

rate.reasoning: Insufficient evidence for the comparison the question asks about: no source read compares designer with prescribed benzodiazepines, and neither has a count of the people who used them, so neither gives a risk per use. The descriptive findings start low (poison-centre records and case reports), are downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness (bounded at very low), and are never upgraded. Status replicated: two independent sources, a national US poison-centre series and a review of case reports from eight countries that does not include that series, agree in direction (mostly sedation; deaths without other drugs rare); each figure comes from one source, and the review cites the poison-centre study only for the point that many people exposed may have no serious effects. The share of death entries listing an opioid is the editors' count of the review's table (115 of 141; 111 of 137 counting each apparent double entry once), which the review itself does not give; it describes which drugs were found together in reported deaths, not whether the combination caused them.
rate.population: People reported to US poison centres after an intentional exposure to a single coded designer benzodiazepine, 2014–2017 (234 reports); people in published case reports and forensic series up to March 2021, as compiled in one review (141 death entries, 63 impaired drivers and 44 emergency admissions; Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA)
rate.exposure: Designer benzodiazepines (mostly etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam), as named by callers and coded (poison centres) or found by forensic analysis (case reports), alone or with other drugs
rate.comparator: None: no comparison with prescribed benzodiazepines or with people who used designer benzodiazepines without harm; within the review's table, death entries with and without other drugs (editors' count)
rate.outcome: Clinical effects, treatments, level of care, graded outcome, duration and deaths coded by poison centres; deaths, impaired driving and emergency admissions in published reports, with the other drugs found
rate.magnitude: Carpenter et al. (2019), NPDS 2014–2017: 474 exposures; 234 intentional single-agent exposures analysed (etizolam 162, clonazolam 50, flubromazolam 13, diclazepam 4, flubromazepam 3, meclonazepam 1, norflurazepam 1); per year 26, 30, 66, 112 (etizolam alone 26, 30, 46, 60; other agents coded only from 2016); median age 25 (13–63); men 86%; suspected suicide 42 (18%). Of 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), confusion 32 (14%), agitated/irritable 22 (9%; text 14%), ataxia 21 (9%), tachycardia 20 (9%), hypotension 19 (8%), coma 10 (4%; text 8%), bradycardia 9 (4%); intubation 7 (3%). Disposition, 224 recorded (editors' sum): treated and released 92 (41%), non-critical admission 31 (14%), critical care 49 (22%), psychiatric facility 36 (16%), lost to follow-up or left 16 (7%). Outcome: major effect 9 (4%), death 1 (0.4%). Duration under 24 h 151 of 178 (84.8%, editors' sum; text 85%). No intervals; no laboratory confirmation. Brunetti et al. (2021), published reports to March 2021: 254 cases (141 deaths, 63 DUID, 44 ED, 3 outpatient, 2 self-administration, 1 drug offence); deaths phenazepam 60, flualprazolam 38, etizolam 34, flubromazolam 4, five others 1 each. Editors' count of the Table 1 death entries: any opioid 115 of 141 (81.6%; etizolam 29 of 34, flualprazolam 27 of 38, phenazepam 53 of 60, flubromazolam 3 of 4, others 3 of 5; methadone 51, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine 49), loperamide or its metabolite 2, no other substance 3; four apparent double entries, all with an opioid: 111 of 137 (81.0%) counting each once.
rate.short: Nobody has tested that. Of 141 deaths with a designer benzo in published reports, 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.
rate.rate: Reports of people who got sick or died, with no count of everyone who used. The poison-centre drugs were never lab-checked, and the deaths come from a review of case reports.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious (card sc_koski_2003: ROBINS-E very high). The comparison is unadjusted, between two groups of people who died that differ in what most plausibly sets the alcohol level at death: age (mean 53 against 48), sex (88 against 67 in 100 men), manner of death (no suicide among the 615 alcohol-only deaths, 11 of the 57 with temazepam) and, unmeasured, tolerance and drinking pattern. Group membership rests on the certified cause; low concentrations of other benzodiazepines were allowed in the drug groups only (30 in 100 of the temazepam deaths), and the authors' statement that they did not change the medians comes without numbers; temazepam was counted from 0.1 mg/L where the other drugs started at their therapeutic range; every concentration was measured after death; 19 tests were run without correction. The difference is statistically clear (P < 0.001; the plotted interval does not include zero), but these differences between the groups could produce it without any effect of temazepam.

inconsistency.note: One study carries the comparison, so consistency across studies cannot be judged; inside it, the concentration split and the analysis without the below-range deaths point the same way.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one benzodiazepine (temazepam), deaths certified as poisoning in Finland, and blood alcohol at death as the outcome, which the statement names. The statement does not extend the finding to alprazolam (Xanax) or to other benzodiazepines, and it says that the risk for living people, which is what people ask, was not measured.

imprecision.note: 57 against 615 deaths; the interval read from Figure 1, about −1.0 to −0.6, excludes zero. An interval is printed as text only for the analysis without the below-range deaths (2.1 to 2.5).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: a retrospective records analysis with no protocol; the authors' companion paper on other benzodiazepines was not read.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the split by temazepam concentration is unadjusted, and deliberate overdoses may sit in the higher half (26 of the 57 above the quoted therapeutic range).

rate.reasoning: Observational records of deaths certified as poisoning: starts low; risk of bias −2 gives very low (the floor). The claim is worded as an association among people who died; the authors' reading of it as a combined toxic effect is reported, not adopted, and no risk is stated, because none can be computed without the people who took both and lived. The breathing sentences rest on one narrative review that shows no data for them (said to be second-hand in the statement) and on a general statement in the Finnish paper; they qualify the claim and are not rated. The review's pharmacokinetic table and its list of 39 published deaths are its author's selections, with no stated search and no appraisal (card sc_tanaka_2002), and are described as such; the published deaths have no comparison group and are not counted as replication. Status single study: one records study carries the comparison; the authors' 2002 paper on other benzodiazepines and the 1980s post-mortem studies of other drugs with alcohol that they cite were not read. Risk facts only: amounts appear as study conditions and measurements after death, never as guidance.
rate.population: People who died in Finland in 1995–2000 whose deaths were investigated toxicologically at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, with the cause certified by a forensic pathologist as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (1006 deaths; 615 from alcohol alone, mean age 53, 88% men; 57 from alcohol with temazepam, mean age 48, 67% men); for the review's material, published single-dose studies of alcohol with a benzodiazepine and 39 published deaths with both in the blood, selected by one author
rate.exposure: Temazepam found in femoral blood after death (counted from 0.1 mg/L, below the bottom of its quoted therapeutic range, 0.4 mg/L) together with alcohol at 0.50 parts per thousand or more, the death certified as poisoning by alcohol, temazepam or both; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam allowed; amounts taken, timing and route unknown. In the review, alcohol given with single benzodiazepine doses in studies (conditions as printed), and both found in published deaths
rate.comparator: Deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol alone, with no other substance found in the screens (615); within the temazepam group, the half with the lower against the half with the higher temazepam concentration; no living people and no adjustment
rate.outcome: Median blood alcohol concentration after death (parts per thousand, mass per mass, femoral blood), compared by Mann–Whitney tests; in the review, a statement on breathing with no measurement reported, and pharmacokinetic measures from single-dose studies
rate.magnitude: Koski et al. (2003), Table 3 (p. 284), median blood alcohol after death in parts per thousand (quartiles; range): alcohol only, n = 615, 3.3 (2.8–3.8; 1.0–6.2); alcohol with temazepam, n = 57, 2.5 (2.0–3.0; 0.7–4.3); printed point estimate of the difference between medians 0.8 (24%), Mann–Whitney P < 0.001 (method not named; here equal to 3.3 − 2.5); 95% interval only in Figure 1, about −1.0 to −0.6 (editors' reading against the axis ticks). The Results text gives 0.6–0.7 for the zopiclone, levomepromazine and temazepam groups, which matches neither Table 3 (0.6, 0.9, 0.8) nor the differences of the printed medians (0.6, 0.7, 0.8). Temazepam split at 0.7 mg/L (Table 4, p. 285): 28 deaths at or below, median 2.9; 29 above, 2.1; printed difference 0.9 (the medians differ by 0.8), P < 0.001. Without the 18 deaths with temazepam under 0.4 mg/L: median 2.2 (95% CI 2.1–2.5) in 39 (Results, p. 283). Temazepam concentrations (Table 2, p. 283): median 0.8 mg/L against a quoted therapeutic range of 0.4–0.9; below the range 18, within it 13, above it 26 (46%); other benzodiazepines at low concentration in 30% of the temazepam group. Groups (Table 1, p. 283): alcohol only, 544 of 615 men (88%), mean age 53 (23–85), 614 accidental (99.8%), no suicide; temazepam, 38 of 57 men (67%), mean age 48 (32–72), 36 accidental (63%), 11 suicides (19%); listed as alcohol poisoning 33 (printed as 46%; 33 of 57 is 58%, editors' calculation) and as drug poisoning 24 (42%). Other drugs, printed differences: citalopram 0.3 (P > 0.05), diltiazem 0.6 (P = 0.006), zopiclone 0.6, levomepromazine 0.9, amitriptyline 1.5, propoxyphene 1.6, doxepin 1.6, promazine 1.9 (each P < 0.001). Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day; Table 5, p. 285): temazepam 0.9 (95% CI 0.7–1.1; 14.33 deaths a year, about 86 over the six years, editors' calculation, so more than the 57 with alcohol) and zopiclone 0.9 (0.7–1.2), the lowest of nine; promazine 120.8 (97.7–143.9). Tanaka (2002), Table 3 (p. 71), eight single-dose arms with alcohol, study conditions as printed: 'unchanged' in five (alprazolam 0.5 and 2 mg by mouth with ethanol 0.8 g/kg, plasma concentration; diazepam 5 mg with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg drunk 3 hours later; diazepam 10 mg with an ethanol infusion; triazolam 0.5 mg with 25 g), 'decreased' in two (brotizolam 0.25 mg with 24 g: Cmax, half-life and clearance; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg: plasma concentration) and 'increased' in one (triazolam 0.5 mg after an ethanol loading regimen: area under the curve, mean 21%); the column is headed 'Benzodiazepine Metabolism' with the measure in brackets, so whether 'decreased' and 'increased' refer to metabolism or to the measure is not stated. No breathing figure anywhere in the review. Table 4 (p. 72): 39 deaths (editors' count; no total printed) from 10 reports (references 49–58), 25 from Joynt (1993); 32 rows name triazolam; blood ethanol 0.1–3.2 mg/mL (editors' median 1.7); triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL, the top of the range the table quotes from one case report, in 13 of the 32 (editors' count, one trace included); alprazolam in 3 rows (200 ng/mL with triazolam and others; a trace with triazolam, diazepam and nordiazepam; 210 ng/mL with others).
rate.short: Death records suggest so. In Finland, people who died with alcohol and the benzo temazepam had less alcohol in their blood. It was about a quarter less than in deaths from alcohol alone.
rate.rate: One study of death records, where the people compared differed in age, sex and suicide, and nothing was adjusted for that. The breathing claim comes from a review that shows no data for it.

risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the association as worded: people starting each drug compared with each other, matched on many claims variables (largest standardized difference 0.02), with similar unadjusted, adjusted and matched estimates (1.44, 1.55, 1.65), near-null negative-control outcomes and a bias analysis for cannabis (ROBINS-I moderate on card sc_moran_2019). What remains, unrecorded substance use, early symptoms, family history, prescriber choice and follow-up ended at a switch (more often after methylphenidate), is named in the statement; whether amphetamine itself causes the difference is not rated.

inconsistency.note: One study; the authors report the higher rate in both databases (database results only in the unread supplement).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds starting prescribed stimulants for ADHD, the first months of use, psychosis treated with an antipsychotic; the statement says it does not cover public insurance, other ages, longer use, dose or use without a prescription.

imprecision.note: 343 events; the hazard ratio's interval (1.31 to 2.09) excludes no difference; the absolute rates are given.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study; no registration is reported, but the primary analysis was prespecified before unblinding of exposure status and unadjusted, adjusted and matched estimates are all printed.

rate.reasoning: Observational (a claims cohort) starts low (METHODS §6.3); no domain downgraded and no upgrade (hazard ratio below 2; no dose data). Low for the statement as worded: in commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds starting a prescribed stimulant for ADHD, new psychosis treated with an antipsychotic was rare in the first months (about 1 in 650 people; 1.78 and 2.83 per 1,000 person-years) and occurred at a higher rate after starting amphetamine (hazard ratio 1.65; about 1 extra episode per 1,000 person-years). The paper's closing description of the risk as about twice as high is not used: it rests on crude shares inflated by longer follow-up after amphetamine. Status single study: no replication is among the papers on file, and the two network meta-analyses of trials read in this round did not study psychosis.
rate.population: 337,919 people aged 13 to 25 with an outpatient ADHD diagnosis in two US commercial insurance claims databases (Optum Clinformatics, IBM MarketScan) who newly started a prescribed stimulant between January 2004 and September 2015, without earlier psychosis, bipolar disorder or antipsychotic use; 221,846 after 1:1 propensity-score matching (mean age about 17; about 37% female)
rate.exposure: Starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine), as dispensed by an outpatient pharmacy; follow-up from day 7 after the first dispensing to 60 days after the end of supply, a switch to the other stimulant, psychosis or the end of data (dose not recorded)
rate.comparator: Starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate), matched 1:1 on a propensity score within each database
rate.outcome: A new psychotic episode: a new diagnosis code for psychosis with an antipsychotic prescription the same day or within 60 days (validated against records reviewed by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug), as incidence per 1,000 person-years and hazard ratio
rate.magnitude: Moran et al. (2019). Matched population (primary, prespecified): 221,846 people (110,923 per group), 143,286 person-years; 343 episodes (2.4 per 1000 person-years); methylphenidate 106 (0.10%), amphetamine 237 (0.21%); incidence 1.78 against 2.83 per 1000 person-years; pooled hazard ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09). Editors' calculations: 343 of 221,846 = 1 in 647 (paper: approximately 1 in 660); rate ratio 2.83/1.78 = 1.59; rate difference 1.05 per 1000 person-years (paper: approximately 1); person-years implied by the printed counts and rates 106/1.78 = about 59,600 and 237/2.83 = about 83,700 (sum about 143,300; printed 143,286); crude ratio from the counts 237/106 = 2.2. Median follow-up: Optum 155 (IQR 82 to 318) against 113 (82 to 209) days; MarketScan 162 (82 to 339) against 123 (82 to 228). Median time to the episode 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Full cohort (337,919: 119,708 and 218,211): 120 (0.10%) against 429 (0.20%); unadjusted HR 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77); adjusted 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92). Stricter definitions (matched): 89 (0.08%) against 211 (0.19%), HR 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), PPV 96.7%; 71 (0.06%) against 163 (0.15%), HR 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22), PPV 98.2%. Post hoc: 13 to 17 years 1.62 (1.24 to 2.12); 18 to 25 years 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00); family or internal medicine 1.78 (1.21 to 2.62); paediatricians 1.70 (1.09 to 2.67); psychiatrists 1.38 (0.93 to 2.04); extended-release only 1.77 (1.30 to 2.40); lisdexamfetamine against extended-release methylphenidate 1.54 (1.10 to 2.16); immediate-release 1.32 (0.77 to 2.29). Negative controls at 100 days: alcohol use disorder 1.12 (0.95 to 1.33), other substance use disorders 1.10 (0.95 to 1.29), cannabis 1.12 (0.91 to 1.38), opioids 0.91 (0.63 to 1.33), depression without psychotic features 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27). Bias analysis: cannabis use among amphetamine starters would need to be 97.0% (against 35.8%, relative risk 2.0 assumed). Switching: 16,489 of 119,708 (13.8%) and 12,233 of 218,211 (5.6%).
rate.short: A bit, in one big US study. But it's rare either way. Each year, about 3 in 1,000 people on amphetamine (as in Adderall) had it, against 2 on methylphenidate.
rate.rate: One large records study, which matched people on many things and checked other explanations. But it isn't a trial, so differences the records missed, like drug use, could explain part of it.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, block-randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data (card sc_straumann_2023: RoB 2 some concerns). Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective; the unwanted-effect scores, complaint counts and ratings are self-reports, and blinding was partial: the dummy and MDMA alone were named correctly in 83 to 100 in 100 sessions, while LSD alone and the combination were often taken for each other (Supplementary Table S8); allocation concealment is not described; the paper's statements on nausea disagree (the supplement's counts fit the results text, not the discussion); the complaint counts were not tested; and the text leaves out LSD's effect on MDMA's levels.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one pair of doses taken together, healthy screened volunteers with limited drug experience, a calm hospital room, which the statement says; it claims nothing about party settings, other doses or timing, or rare harms.

imprecision.note: 24 people. The rises in blood pressure and heart rate against LSD alone are significant, but the findings that temperature and unwanted effects were no higher, or no lower, than with LSD alone are non-significant comparisons, not shown equivalence, and rare harms such as serotonin toxicity cannot be detected in 24 people. The longer duration with both drugs rests on one test at p < 0.05, and the complaint counts were not tested.

rate.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim gives how long the effects lasted, as measured, but leaves out how strong the good effects felt, and gives no timing or dosing advice. The online supplement, read in round pdf-2026-11-26, settles the nausea counts and adds the duration and complaint counts; it does not change the rating.
rate.population: 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25 to 54), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 12 had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before (1 to 13 times); excluded were more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted), a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder and interfering medicines; Basel
rate.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules; analysed 25.40 mg each) and LSD base 100 µg (oral solution; analysed content 92.5 µg) taken at the same time, double-blind and double-dummy, in a calm hospital room with one investigator (study conditions)
rate.comparator: LSD 100 µg alone, MDMA 100 mg alone and placebo in the same people, at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order
rate.outcome: Peak blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours, self-rated bad drug effect, fear and nausea, and adverse events; blood levels of LSD and MDMA over 24 hours
rate.magnitude: Straumann et al. rate.reasoning: A cross-sectional self-report survey starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). rate.population: People going through opioid withdrawal in custody (jails and prisons in the United Kingdom and the United States), as described in one editorial
rate.exposure: Opioid withdrawal (from heroin and other opioids) without adequate medical management
rate.comparator: None (reported cases; no comparison group and no denominator)
rate.outcome: Death during withdrawal, as reported in the press and in a court case (causes as the editorial gives them)

rate.rate: One editorial, using cases from news reports, a court case and a prosecutor's letter, all in custody, with no medical details. Nobody counted how many people went through withdrawal, so how often it kills is unknown.

item.statement: Scientists have measured how MDMA affects peeing.
item.why: No study has. They measured a water-holding hormone and blood salt instead, and the one team that collected urine never reported what it found.

lines.short: Nobody knows: no study has measured it. A water-holding hormone rose in 8 men on MDMA. Three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker.
lines.but: None of these studies reported anything about pee. So nobody knows if the hormone has anything to do with it.
how: In 8 healthy men, the body's water-holding hormone rose 1 to 2 hours after one MDMA capsule. Only 3 of them also had a day without MDMA, and the study didn't test the difference.
In three studies, the same people took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another (16, 12 and 32 people). The hormone, or a marker released with it, didn't rise.

Blood salt fell a little after MDMA, and more when people drank a lot of water at once. The team that found this collected urine too, but never reported what it found. Low blood salt has its own answer.

The only case of someone who couldn't pee at all: a 19-year-old man, for 24 hours, after saying he'd taken 15 tablets in 36 hours. A tube drained his bladder. Nobody tested him or the pills for drugs.

item.statement: Most deaths linked to designer benzos involved no other drug.
item.why: In a review of published cases, 115 of 141 death entries also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.

lines.short: Nobody has tested that. Of 141 deaths with a designer benzo in published reports, 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.
lines.but: These reports only count people who got into trouble, not everyone who used. So they can't say how risky one use is.
how: US poison centres, 2014 to 2017: in 234 reports naming a designer benzo and no other drug, mostly etizolam, 65 in 100 people were drowsy and 3 in 100 needed a breathing tube. One man died.
Nobody lab-tested which drug these people took. Reports rose from 26 to 112 a year, partly because new drugs got their own codes in 2016.

A review of published cases to 2021 found 141 death entries, mostly phenazepam, flualprazolam and etizolam. 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug. A few people seem to be listed twice.
Designer benzos have turned up in fake Xanax pills, and buyers often don't know what's in them.

item.statement: In death records, people who had temazepam too died with less alcohol in their blood.
item.why: In Finland: 2.5 parts per thousand in the middle, against 3.3 in deaths from alcohol alone. But only deaths were counted, and the groups were different people, so it can't show the risk.

lines.short: Death records suggest so. In Finland, people who died with alcohol and the benzo temazepam had less alcohol in their blood. It was about a quarter less than in deaths from alcohol alone.
lines.but: Only deaths were counted, and the two groups were different kinds of people. So this can't show how risky mixing is.
how: Finnish death records, 1995 to 2000: in 615 deaths from alcohol alone, the middle blood alcohol level was 3.3 parts per thousand. In 57 deaths with alcohol and temazepam, it was 2.5. Those with more temazepam had died at lower alcohol levels still.
The groups weren't alike, and nothing was adjusted for that. The alcohol-only deaths were older and more often men, and none was a suicide; 11 of the 57 temazepam deaths were.

A 2002 review says high doses of alcohol and benzos together slow breathing more than the two add up to. But it shows no breathing data for that. In 5 of the 8 single-dose tests it lists, alcohol didn't change benzo blood levels, Xanax's included.

Temazepam was the only benzo studied in the death records. For Xanax, there's one blood-level test and 3 published deaths, all with other drugs too. None of these studies measured breathing, or the risk for living people who mix.

item.statement: In a US survey, over 1 in 3 people who took buprenorphine (as in Suboxone) after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal.
item.why: 250 of 685 did (37 in 100), against 15 in 100 after methadone. These were memories, and the survey couldn't tell withdrawal buprenorphine caused from withdrawal it didn't ease.

lines.short: Many say so. In a US survey, 37 in 100 who took Suboxone's main drug after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal. After methadone, 15 in 100 did.
lines.but: These are memories, not records. And the survey couldn't tell if Suboxone caused the withdrawal or just didn't ease it.
how: 1,163 people starting treatment at 49 US centres said they'd used fentanyl. 685 had taken buprenorphine, Suboxone's main drug, within a month after fentanyl. 250 of them remembered severe withdrawal.

The shorter the shortest wait they reported after fentanyl, the more often they remembered it: about 45 in 100 under a day, 34 in 100 at 1 to 2 days, about 25 in 100 at 2 days to a week, 14 in 100 at a week to a month. There was no clear cut-off.
The paper's summary says 22 in 100 for those who waited under a day. That's out of all 685 people. Out of the 339 who waited under a day, it's 45 in 100.
Nothing else that differed between people was taken into account. The dose, the form and who gave it weren't asked.

item.statement: Starting Adderall instead of Ritalin doubles the risk of psychosis.
item.why: In one big records study it was about 1.65 times the rate, about 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. 'Twice' came from leaving out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

lines.short: A bit, in one big US study. But it's rare either way. Each year, about 3 in 1,000 people on amphetamine (as in Adderall) had it, against 2 on methylphenidate.
lines.but: It's one study of insurance records, not a trial. Things the records missed, like drug use or early signs of illness, could explain part of it.
how: It used records of about 222,000 young people, aged 13 to 25, with ADHD and US insurance. They had started either medicine and were matched on what the records showed.
Over about 4 to 5 months, 343 had a new psychotic episode treated with antipsychotic medicine, about 1 in 650. Per 1,000 people a year, that's 1.8 on methylphenidate and 2.8 on amphetamine.
That's about 1.65 times the rate, or 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. The paper's own summary, about twice the risk, leaves out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

Counting psychosis more strictly gave similar results. Emergency or hospital care for alcohol or cannabis wasn't more common after amphetamine. Records can't show the dose, missed drug use, or if pills were taken.

item.statement: Taking MDMA with LSD pushes heart rate and blood pressure higher than LSD alone.
item.why: In a lab study of 24 people, they rose about as high as on MDMA alone. Body temperature wasn't clearly higher.

lines.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
lines.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.

Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone, and more people had trembling, restless legs or teeth grinding. Nausea in the first 12 hours: 11 of 24 with both, 14 on MDMA alone, 7 on LSD alone, 4 on the dummy. Nobody had a serious problem.

The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later. The effects lasted about an hour and a half longer than on LSD alone, and the longest lasted 21 hours.

item.statement: You can't die from opioid withdrawal.
item.why: Deaths have been reported, all in jail; one editorial suggests untreated vomiting and diarrhoea can dry the body out. How often it happens is unknown.

lines.short: Deaths have been reported, but nobody knows how often. One editorial lists 11, all in jail. It suggests vomiting and diarrhoea, left untreated, can dry the body out until the heart fails.
lines.but: It's one editorial's short list, from the news, a court case and a prosecutor's letter. It has no medical details. And nobody counted how many went through withdrawal, so there's no rate.
how: The authors' idea: vomiting and diarrhoea that don't stop, left untreated, dry the body out. Blood sodium rises, and the heart can fail.

The cases: a woman in custody in the UK in 1998, and 10 people in US jails from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49. For those 10, the list gives only the year, sex, age, place and a news source (for one, a prosecutor's letter).
The authors say each death came slowly, with time to treat it, and call the deaths neglect or a lack of medical care. Their list gives no medical details to check this.
They say such deaths are rising but give no counts over time. Nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.
