lines.statement: In people who take MDMA, evidence is insufficient to say how often passing urine becomes difficult, or why: no study read here measured difficulty passing urine or reported the amount of urine passed or how the bladder worked after MDMA, and the only report read of someone unable to pass urine is a single case. In that case, a healthy 19-year-old man was referred to a hospital urology team in the UK after 24 hours of acute retention of urine: apart from a painful bladder that could be felt, examination and a routine urine test were normal; a catheter drained the bladder and was removed after 36 hours, and the retention did not come back (how long he was followed is not stated). By his own account he had used only ecstasy in the previous 12 months, one or two tablets once or twice a week, usually at parties, and he later said he had taken 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission (as reported, not a recommendation); neither he nor the tablets were tested for any drug, and when he took the last tablet is not given. His doctors wrote that the drug had 'almost certainly' caused the retention, reasoning that MDMA stimulates the alpha-adrenergic nerve fibres that can close the bladder neck; nothing was measured in him to test this, no other cause was looked for beyond the examination, and the only earlier urinary complication they knew of was an urgent need to pass urine (second-hand, from a 1986 report) (Bryden et al., 1995). The controlled studies read measured the body's water balance, not passing urine. In 8 healthy men aged 22 to 32 given one capsule of MDMA (47.5 mg of the hydrochloride, equal to 40 mg of MDMA base, with 200 mL of water; study conditions), antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), the hormone that tells the body to hold back water, peaked 1 to 2 hours later, from a range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L before the dose to 2.46 to 9.16 pmol/L at 2 hours (one-tailed p = 0.006), and blood sodium fell by 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of the 8 (one-tailed p = 0.025); the only comparison was 3 of the same men on a later, untreated occasion, not compared statistically, and no urine was measured (Henry et al., 1998). In two double-blind studies in which healthy people who had taken MDMA before had MDMA (1.5 mg/kg of the hydrochloride; study condition) and a placebo on different days (Baggott et al., 2016), MDMA did not raise the hormone in 16 people whose drinking was limited to about 473 mL an hour (z = 1.21, p = 0.589), while prazosin, a medicine that lowers blood pressure, given as a check because it releases the hormone, did; and in 12 people who drank 20 mL/kg of water an hour after the capsule, neither the hormone (p = 0.74) nor copeptin, a marker released with it (p = 0.89), rose. In a third double-blind crossover study, of 32 healthy volunteers given 125 mg (study condition), copeptin measured before and 1 and 2 hours after the dose did not change (no statistic printed; Hysek et al., 2014). Blood sodium did fall after MDMA in Baggott's studies: by less than 2 mmol/L at its lowest against placebo when drinking was limited, and further after the water load than after the same water load with placebo (lowest value, F(1,9) = 13.2, p = 0.005; means about 133.6 against 137.7 mmol/L at 3 hours; both editors' approximate readings of the paper's figures), with one woman reaching 127 mmol/L without symptoms; two people who vomited soon after drinking the water in their MDMA session were left out. The authors could not explain the fall by the hormone, copeptin or drug levels, and did not establish a mechanism. They collected urine before the dose and over 0 to 8 and 8 to 24 hours after it, but report no urine result, and list not measuring urine concentration (osmolality) as a limitation. All these volunteers were healthy and took a single known dose given by researchers in a research setting. Where a larger fall in blood sodium can lead (seizures, brain swelling and deaths, reported mostly in young people) is a separate answer (see the answer on whether drinking lots of water on MDMA can lead to low blood salt). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who take MDMA: one healthy 19-year-old man treated by a hospital urology team in the UK (case report); in laboratory studies, 8 healthy men aged 22 to 32 in London (Henry et al., 1998), 16 people (8 women, 8 men; aged 18 to 42) and 12 people (6 women, 6 men; aged 21 to 40) in the USA, all healthy and with earlier MDMA use (Baggott et al., 2016), and 32 healthy volunteers in Basel (16 women, 16 men; aged 20 to 31; 22 had never taken MDMA) (Hysek et al., 2014)
lines.exposure: MDMA: in the case, tablets sold as ecstasy, 15 in the 36 hours before admission by the man's own account, content untested (as reported, not a recommendation); in the laboratory, a single oral dose given by researchers (study conditions): 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL of water (Henry), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride with drinking limited to about 473 mL an hour or followed an hour later by 20 mL/kg of water drunk within 30 minutes (Baggott), or 125 mg (Hysek)
lines.comparator: None in the case report; each man's own values before the dose, and 3 of the men on a later untreated occasion, not compared statistically (Henry); placebo in the same people on another day, double-blind (Baggott, Hysek), with prazosin as a check drug in Baggott's first study and the same water load after placebo in the second
lines.outcome: Difficulty passing urine, urine volume and bladder function (not measured or not reported in any study read; one case of acute retention of urine described); antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) and copeptin; blood sodium
lines.magnitude: Bryden et al. (1995), one case: man aged 19; acute retention for 24 hours before referral; painful palpable bladder; examination and urinalysis otherwise normal; urethral catheter removed after 36 hours on free drainage; no further retention (follow-up length not stated); self-reported use: only ecstasy in the previous 12 months, one or two tablets once or twice a week, then 15 tablets in the 36 hours before admission (earlier amphetamine and cannabis); no drug screen, no tablet analysis, no residual volume, flow study or imaging. Henry et al. (1998), 8 healthy men aged 22-32, 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) with 200 mL water at 10:00: vasopressin range 1.14-1.88 pmol/L before and 2.46-9.16 at 2 hours (paired t test, one-tailed p = 0.006; about 0.012 two-tailed, editors' calculation), maximum between 1 and 2 hours, against a small decrease on 3 later untreated occasions (not compared statistically); sodium 139-145 mmol/L before and 140-142 at 2 hours, down 1-3 in 7 of 8 and up 1 in one (one-tailed p = 0.025; about 0.05 two-tailed, editors' calculation); urine not measured. Baggott et al. (2016), 1.5 mg/kg MDMA hydrochloride (1.26 mg/kg base) or placebo, double-blind, within person, sequence- and gender-balanced: Study 1 (16 people, 8 women; water limited to about 473 mL an hour; 1213 +/- 76 mL drunk in 8 hours, not differing by condition): maximum ADH by condition F(3,45) = 5.68, p = 0.002; prazosin alone z = 3.46 (p = 0.002), prazosin with MDMA z = 3.22 (p = 0.004), MDMA alone z = 1.21 (p = 0.589); minimum sodium by condition F(3,357) = 8.44 (p < 0.0001), MDMA alone t(357) = -4.05 (p < 0.0001), MDMA with prazosin t(357) = -3.50 (p = 0.0005), prazosin alone no effect; MDMA curves under 2 mmol/L below placebo at their lowest, around 3 hours (editors' approximate reading of Figure 3a). Study 2 (12 people, 6 women; 20 mL/kg water within 30 minutes, an hour after the capsule; two people who vomited in their MDMA sessions excluded): maximum ADH F(1,15) = 0.113 (p = 0.74), maximum copeptin F(1,9) = 0.019 (p = 0.89); minimum sodium F(1,9) = 13.2 (p = 0.005); means about 133.6 mmol/L at 3 hours after MDMA against about 137.7 after placebo, whose lowest mean was about 136 at 2 hours (editors' approximate readings of Figure 3b); one woman 127 mmol/L at 3 hours, transient, without symptoms. No mean, change or interval is printed for any sodium result. Urine pooled before dosing and over 0-8 and 8-24 hours; no urine result reported. Hysek et al. (2014), 32 healthy volunteers (16 women), 125 mg against placebo, double-blind crossover: copeptin before and 1 and 2 hours after not altered (no statistic printed). No study gives a frequency of difficulty passing urine.
lines.reasoning: The only evidence on the claim's outcome, difficulty passing urine, is one case report: observational, starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness (the controlled studies measured a hormone and blood sodium, not passing urine) and one for imprecision; very low (the floor). Relation: insufficient evidence, because no study read measured how often passing urine becomes difficult after MDMA, or why. The placebo-controlled studies (Baggott et al., 2016; Hysek et al., 2014) would start high for their own outcomes, but they do not measure this claim's outcome and so do not raise it; their finding of no rise in the hormone or copeptin disagrees with the uncontrolled rise in 8 men (Henry et al., 1998), and the statement reports both without choosing an explanation. The alpha-adrenergic account is the case authors' reasoning, and no study read tested the hormone against urine; neither account is asserted. Status: single study (one case report on passing urine). Amounts appear only as each study's conditions, and the claim gives no advice on amounts or fluid.

lines.q: Why is it hard to pee on MDMA?
lines.short: Nobody knows: no study has measured it. A water-holding hormone rose in 8 men on MDMA. Three studies with a dummy pill found no rise in it or its marker.
lines.but: None of these studies reported anything about pee. So nobody knows if the hormone has anything to do with it.
how: In 8 healthy men, the body's water-holding hormone rose 1 to 2 hours after one MDMA capsule. Only 3 of them also had a day without MDMA, and the study didn't test the difference.
In three studies, the same people took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another (16, 12 and 32 people). The hormone, or a marker released with it, didn't rise.

Blood salt fell a little after MDMA, and more when people drank a lot of water at once. The team that found this collected urine too, but never reported what it found. Low blood salt has its own answer.

The only case of someone who couldn't pee at all: a 19-year-old man, for 24 hours, after saying he'd taken 15 tablets in 36 hours. A tube drained his bladder. Nobody tested him or the pills for drugs.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether designer benzodiazepines (benzodiazepines and close relatives sold on the illicit market, such as etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam, of which etizolam and phenazepam are licensed medicines in a few countries) are more dangerous than prescribed benzodiazepines: no source read here compares them, and neither source counts the people who used them without coming to attention, so neither gives a risk per use. In US poison-centre records (the National Poison Data System), 474 exposures to designer benzodiazepines were reported from 2014 to 2017; the 234 intentional exposures to one of 11 coded designer benzodiazepines and no other substance were analysed, while the reports involving other substances, about half, were neither collected nor analysed (Carpenter et al., 2019). The 234 were mostly etizolam (162) and clonazolam (50); the median age was 25, 86% were men, and 42 (18 in 100) were coded as suspected suicide. Drowsiness or lethargy was coded in 152 (65 in 100), slurred speech in 40 (17), confusion in 32 (14), agitation or irritability in 22 (9), a fast heart rate in 20 (9), low blood pressure in 19 (8) and coma in 10 (4), as the table gives them (the text gives 14% for agitation and 8% for coma), and 7 people (3 in 100) were intubated. Of the 224 whose care was recorded (editors' sum), 92 (41 in 100) were treated and released, 31 (14 in 100) admitted to a non-critical-care ward, 49 (22 in 100) to critical care and 36 (16 in 100) to a psychiatric facility; 9 (4 in 100) had a major effect, and one man, aged 29, died after a reported intentional ingestion of etizolam (1 of 234, 0.4%); effects lasted less than a day in 151 of the 178 with a recorded duration (85 in 100; editors' sum of the table's rows). The drug in each report is the one named by the caller and coded by poison-centre staff, with no laboratory confirmation, and the authors say people may have taken other compounds than those coded; they expect people without significant symptoms to have gone unreported, so that the reports undercount exposures and overstate severity; and a death after flubromazolam, coded under the general 'benzodiazepine' code, was missing from the data. Reports rose from 26 in 2014 to 112 in 2017, a 330% increase that the abstract reads as rising incidence, but only etizolam had its own code before 2016: etizolam alone went from 26 to 60 reports. In published case reports and forensic series up to March 2021, as compiled in a review that did not appraise them (Brunetti et al., 2021; so these figures are second-hand), 12 designer benzodiazepines appear in 141 death entries, 63 cases of impaired driving and 44 emergency admissions, from eight countries; the deaths were mostly with phenazepam (60), flualprazolam (38) and etizolam (34). By the editors' count of the review's table, 115 of the 141 death entries also list at least one opioid (methadone in 51, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine in 49), 2 more list loperamide or its metabolite, and 3 list no other drug; at least four people appear to be listed twice, all four with an opioid, and counting each of them once gives 111 of 137 (editors' calculation), about 8 in 10 either way. The two deaths in which, by the review's text, phenazepam alone was listed as the cause list alcohol in one and diazepam with dihydrocodeine in the other. In the emergency cases the review describes mostly sedation (depression of the central nervous system), and agitation and delirium in a few (editors' summary of its drug-by-drug text); its authors say that because several drugs are usually present, a death often cannot be assigned to one of them, and that blood levels overlapped between drivers judged impaired and drivers judged not impaired, and were similar in drivers and in deaths. The review's introduction says that, compared with classical benzodiazepines, these drugs produce strong sedation and amnesia and raise the risk of breathing depression and death with other depressants, citing two papers (a review of how to find information on their potency, and a study of prescribed benzodiazepines taken with opioids by people starting dialysis), and presents no comparison of its own. It also reports, from agency sources, counterfeit Xanax (alprazolam) tablets holding etizolam, flualprazolam or phenazepam seized in the US, Australia, Singapore and Malaysia, flubromazolam first identified in tablets labelled 'XANAX', seven young people treated in emergency departments after taking what they thought was alprazolam (flualprazolam, not confirmed in three), and products holding variable amounts or other drugs, generally without the buyer knowing. What drug checking found in pills and powders sold as something else is in the answers on fake pills and on benzodiazepine test strips. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: People reported to US poison centres after an intentional exposure to a single coded designer benzodiazepine, 2014–2017 (234 reports); people in published case reports and forensic series up to March 2021, as compiled in one review (141 death entries, 63 impaired drivers and 44 emergency admissions; Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA)
lines.exposure: Designer benzodiazepines (mostly etizolam, clonazolam, flualprazolam, flubromazolam and phenazepam), as named by callers and coded (poison centres) or found by forensic analysis (case reports), alone or with other drugs
lines.comparator: None: no comparison with prescribed benzodiazepines or with people who used designer benzodiazepines without harm; within the review's table, death entries with and without other drugs (editors' count)
lines.outcome: Clinical effects, treatments, level of care, graded outcome, duration and deaths coded by poison centres; deaths, impaired driving and emergency admissions in published reports, with the other drugs found
lines.magnitude: Carpenter et al. (2019), NPDS 2014–2017: 474 exposures; 234 intentional single-agent exposures analysed (etizolam 162, clonazolam 50, flubromazolam 13, diclazepam 4, flubromazepam 3, meclonazepam 1, norflurazepam 1); per year 26, 30, 66, 112 (etizolam alone 26, 30, 46, 60; other agents coded only from 2016); median age 25 (13–63); men 86%; suspected suicide 42 (18%). Of 234: drowsiness/lethargy 152 (65%), slurred speech 40 (17%), confusion 32 (14%), agitated/irritable 22 (9%; text 14%), ataxia 21 (9%), tachycardia 20 (9%), hypotension 19 (8%), coma 10 (4%; text 8%), bradycardia 9 (4%); intubation 7 (3%). Disposition, 224 recorded (editors' sum): treated and released 92 (41%), non-critical admission 31 (14%), critical care 49 (22%), psychiatric facility 36 (16%), lost to follow-up or left 16 (7%). Outcome: major effect 9 (4%), death 1 (0.4%). Duration under 24 h 151 of 178 (84.8%, editors' sum; text 85%). No intervals; no laboratory confirmation. Brunetti et al. (2021), published reports to March 2021: 254 cases (141 deaths, 63 DUID, 44 ED, 3 outpatient, 2 self-administration, 1 drug offence); deaths phenazepam 60, flualprazolam 38, etizolam 34, flubromazolam 4, five others 1 each. Editors' count of the Table 1 death entries: any opioid 115 of 141 (81.6%; etizolam 29 of 34, flualprazolam 27 of 38, phenazepam 53 of 60, flubromazolam 3 of 4, others 3 of 5; methadone 51, morphine or 6-acetylmorphine 49), loperamide or its metabolite 2, no other substance 3; four apparent double entries, all with an opioid: 111 of 137 (81.0%) counting each once.
lines.reasoning: Insufficient evidence for the comparison the question asks about: no source read compares designer with prescribed benzodiazepines, and neither has a count of the people who used them, so neither gives a risk per use. The descriptive findings start low (poison-centre records and case reports), are downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness (bounded at very low), and are never upgraded. Status replicated: two independent sources, a national US poison-centre series and a review of case reports from eight countries that does not include that series, agree in direction (mostly sedation; deaths without other drugs rare); each figure comes from one source, and the review cites the poison-centre study only for the point that many people exposed may have no serious effects. The share of death entries listing an opioid is the editors' count of the review's table (115 of 141; 111 of 137 counting each apparent double entry once), which the review itself does not give; it describes which drugs were found together in reported deaths, not whether the combination caused them.

lines.q: Are designer benzos like etizolam more dangerous?
lines.short: Nobody has tested that. Of 141 deaths with a designer benzo in published reports, 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug.
lines.but: These reports only count people who got into trouble, not everyone who used. So they can't say how risky one use is.
how: US poison centres, 2014 to 2017: in 234 reports naming a designer benzo and no other drug, mostly etizolam, 65 in 100 people were drowsy and 3 in 100 needed a breathing tube. One man died.
Nobody lab-tested which drug these people took. Reports rose from 26 to 112 a year, partly because new drugs got their own codes in 2016.

A review of published cases to 2021 found 141 death entries, mostly phenazepam, flualprazolam and etizolam. 115 also listed an opioid, and only 3 listed no other drug. A few people seem to be listed twice.
Designer benzos have turned up in fake Xanax pills, and buyers often don't know what's in them.

lines.statement: In people who died in Finland in 1995–2000 of a poisoning that a forensic pathologist certified as due to alcohol, a single drug or both, deaths in which the benzodiazepine temazepam was found together with alcohol (at least 0.50 parts per thousand), compared with deaths from alcohol alone, were associated with a lower blood alcohol concentration measured after death: median 2.5 against 3.3 parts per thousand by weight (57 against 615 deaths), a difference the paper puts at 0.8 (24%; Mann–Whitney P < 0.001) by a method it does not name, with a 95% interval of about −1.0 to −0.6 that it shows only in a figure (editors' reading; Koski et al., 2003). Within the temazepam group, the half with the higher temazepam concentration had died at the lower blood alcohol (median 2.1 against 2.9; printed difference 0.9, P < 0.001), and setting aside the 18 deaths in which temazepam was below its therapeutic range (under 0.4 mg/L) left a median of 2.2 (95% CI 2.1 to 2.5) in the other 39. The authors read these lower levels as a combined toxic effect of temazepam and alcohol, growing with the temazepam concentration; the pattern fits that reading, but the differences between the groups set out next could also produce it, and the design cannot show any risk. Only people who died were counted, so nobody who took both and lived is in the data, and nothing was adjusted although the groups were unlike: the alcohol-only deaths were older (mean age 53 against 48) and more often men (88 against 67 in 100), and all but one were recorded as accidents, none as a suicide, while 11 of the 57 temazepam deaths were recorded as suicides and 36 as accidents. Which group a death joined depended on the cause the pathologist certified (alcohol poisoning for 33 of the 57 temazepam deaths, alone or as the more important cause, and drug poisoning for 24); low concentrations of other benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide or their breakdown products) were allowed in the drug groups and were found in 30 in 100 of the temazepam deaths but in none of the alcohol-only deaths, which had to be free of every other substance; temazepam was above the therapeutic range the paper quotes in 26 of the 57; and every concentration was measured after death. Of the nine drugs studied this way, temazepam's difference was the fourth smallest (citalopram 0.3, not significant; zopiclone and diltiazem 0.6; levomepromazine 0.9; amitriptyline, propoxyphene, doxepin and promazine 1.5 to 1.9), and temazepam and zopiclone had the lowest fatal toxicity index (deaths per amount sold, 0.9 each); the authors say this ordering reflects how the drugs are used, some taken deliberately in overdose, as well as their own toxicity. Temazepam was the only benzodiazepine among the nine (drugs found in at least 20 such poisonings); the authors' 2002 paper on other benzodiazepines was not read, and alprazolam (Xanax) was not studied. What alcohol and benzodiazepines do to breathing together is described only second-hand: a 2002 narrative review by one author (Tanaka, 2002) states that high doses of the two depress breathing synergistically (more than the sum of each), citing three single-dose studies that its own table describes only by pharmacokinetic measures, and gives no breathing measurement, number or dose for it; the Finnish authors call the combined effect of alcohol and drugs that depress the nervous system generally considered additive and usually not a matter of blood levels (a general statement, not their finding). In the review's table of eight single-dose study arms, alcohol did not change the benzodiazepine's pharmacokinetics in five, alprazolam's among them, and changed them in three, in both directions, although its abstract says that metabolism is in general delayed. The review also lists 39 published deaths in which both alcohol and a benzodiazepine were found (from 10 reports of 1988 to 1999, 25 of them from one Canadian series of triazolam deaths; 3 with alprazolam, each with other drugs), with no count of people who took both and lived. No study read here measured breathing, sedation or how often harm follows in living people who combine alcohol with a benzodiazepine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who died in Finland in 1995–2000 whose deaths were investigated toxicologically at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, with the cause certified by a forensic pathologist as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (1006 deaths; 615 from alcohol alone, mean age 53, 88% men; 57 from alcohol with temazepam, mean age 48, 67% men); for the review's material, published single-dose studies of alcohol with a benzodiazepine and 39 published deaths with both in the blood, selected by one author
lines.exposure: Temazepam found in femoral blood after death (counted from 0.1 mg/L, below the bottom of its quoted therapeutic range, 0.4 mg/L) together with alcohol at 0.50 parts per thousand or more, the death certified as poisoning by alcohol, temazepam or both; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam allowed; amounts taken, timing and route unknown. In the review, alcohol given with single benzodiazepine doses in studies (conditions as printed), and both found in published deaths
lines.comparator: Deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol alone, with no other substance found in the screens (615); within the temazepam group, the half with the lower against the half with the higher temazepam concentration; no living people and no adjustment
lines.outcome: Median blood alcohol concentration after death (parts per thousand, mass per mass, femoral blood), compared by Mann–Whitney tests; in the review, a statement on breathing with no measurement reported, and pharmacokinetic measures from single-dose studies
lines.magnitude: Koski et al. (2003), Table 3 (p. 284), median blood alcohol after death in parts per thousand (quartiles; range): alcohol only, n = 615, 3.3 (2.8–3.8; 1.0–6.2); alcohol with temazepam, n = 57, 2.5 (2.0–3.0; 0.7–4.3); printed point estimate of the difference between medians 0.8 (24%), Mann–Whitney P < 0.001 (method not named; here equal to 3.3 − 2.5); 95% interval only in Figure 1, about −1.0 to −0.6 (editors' reading against the axis ticks). The Results text gives 0.6–0.7 for the zopiclone, levomepromazine and temazepam groups, which matches neither Table 3 (0.6, 0.9, 0.8) nor the differences of the printed medians (0.6, 0.7, 0.8). Temazepam split at 0.7 mg/L (Table 4, p. 285): 28 deaths at or below, median 2.9; 29 above, 2.1; printed difference 0.9 (the medians differ by 0.8), P < 0.001. Without the 18 deaths with temazepam under 0.4 mg/L: median 2.2 (95% CI 2.1–2.5) in 39 (Results, p. 283). Temazepam concentrations (Table 2, p. 283): median 0.8 mg/L against a quoted therapeutic range of 0.4–0.9; below the range 18, within it 13, above it 26 (46%); other benzodiazepines at low concentration in 30% of the temazepam group. Groups (Table 1, p. 283): alcohol only, 544 of 615 men (88%), mean age 53 (23–85), 614 accidental (99.8%), no suicide; temazepam, 38 of 57 men (67%), mean age 48 (32–72), 36 accidental (63%), 11 suicides (19%); listed as alcohol poisoning 33 (printed as 46%; 33 of 57 is 58%, editors' calculation) and as drug poisoning 24 (42%). Other drugs, printed differences: citalopram 0.3 (P > 0.05), diltiazem 0.6 (P = 0.006), zopiclone 0.6, levomepromazine 0.9, amitriptyline 1.5, propoxyphene 1.6, doxepin 1.6, promazine 1.9 (each P < 0.001). Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day; Table 5, p. 285): temazepam 0.9 (95% CI 0.7–1.1; 14.33 deaths a year, about 86 over the six years, editors' calculation, so more than the 57 with alcohol) and zopiclone 0.9 (0.7–1.2), the lowest of nine; promazine 120.8 (97.7–143.9). Tanaka (2002), Table 3 (p. 71), eight single-dose arms with alcohol, study conditions as printed: 'unchanged' in five (alprazolam 0.5 and 2 mg by mouth with ethanol 0.8 g/kg, plasma concentration; diazepam 5 mg with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg drunk 3 hours later; diazepam 10 mg with an ethanol infusion; triazolam 0.5 mg with 25 g), 'decreased' in two (brotizolam 0.25 mg with 24 g: Cmax, half-life and clearance; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg: plasma concentration) and 'increased' in one (triazolam 0.5 mg after an ethanol loading regimen: area under the curve, mean 21%); the column is headed 'Benzodiazepine Metabolism' with the measure in brackets, so whether 'decreased' and 'increased' refer to metabolism or to the measure is not stated. No breathing figure anywhere in the review. Table 4 (p. 72): 39 deaths (editors' count; no total printed) from 10 reports (references 49–58), 25 from Joynt (1993); 32 rows name triazolam; blood ethanol 0.1–3.2 mg/mL (editors' median 1.7); triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL, the top of the range the table quotes from one case report, in 13 of the 32 (editors' count, one trace included); alprazolam in 3 rows (200 ng/mL with triazolam and others; a trace with triazolam, diazepam and nordiazepam; 210 ng/mL with others).
lines.reasoning: Observational records of deaths certified as poisoning: starts low; risk of bias −2 gives very low (the floor). The claim is worded as an association among people who died; the authors' reading of it as a combined toxic effect is reported, not adopted, and no risk is stated, because none can be computed without the people who took both and lived. The breathing sentences rest on one narrative review that shows no data for them (said to be second-hand in the statement) and on a general statement in the Finnish paper; they qualify the claim and are not rated. The review's pharmacokinetic table and its list of 39 published deaths are its author's selections, with no stated search and no appraisal (card sc_tanaka_2002), and are described as such; the published deaths have no comparison group and are not counted as replication. Status single study: one records study carries the comparison; the authors' 2002 paper on other benzodiazepines and the 1980s post-mortem studies of other drugs with alcohol that they cite were not read. Risk facts only: amounts appear as study conditions and measurements after death, never as guidance.

lines.q: Is it dangerous to mix benzos like Xanax with alcohol?
lines.short: Death records suggest so. In Finland, people who died with alcohol and the benzo temazepam had less alcohol in their blood. It was about a quarter less than in deaths from alcohol alone.
lines.but: Only deaths were counted, and the two groups were different kinds of people. So this can't show how risky mixing is.
how: Finnish death records, 1995 to 2000: in 615 deaths from alcohol alone, the middle blood alcohol level was 3.3 parts per thousand. In 57 deaths with alcohol and temazepam, it was 2.5. Those with more temazepam had died at lower alcohol levels still.
The groups weren't alike, and nothing was adjusted for that. The alcohol-only deaths were older and more often men, and none was a suicide; 11 of the 57 temazepam deaths were.

A 2002 review says high doses of alcohol and benzos together slow breathing more than the two add up to. But it shows no breathing data for that. In 5 of the 8 single-dose tests it lists, alcohol didn't change benzo blood levels, Xanax's included.

Temazepam was the only benzo studied in the death records. For Xanax, there's one blood-level test and 3 published deaths, all with other drugs too. None of these studies measured breathing, or the risk for living people who mix.

lines.statement: In 13- to 25-year-olds with ADHD in two US commercial insurance claims databases who started a prescribed stimulant between 2004 and 2015, starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine) compared with starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate) was associated with a higher rate of a new psychotic episode treated with an antipsychotic, although such episodes were rare after either: among 221,846 people matched one to one on a propensity score (110,923 in each group), 343 had an episode over a median follow-up of 113 to 162 days by group and database (about 4 to 5 months), about 1 in 650 (343 of 221,846 is 1 in 647, editors' calculation; the paper says approximately 1 in 660); 106 episodes followed methylphenidate and 237 amphetamine, 1.78 against 2.83 episodes per 1,000 person-years of use, a hazard ratio of 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09), prespecified as the primary analysis, and a difference of about 1 episode per 1,000 person-years (1.05, editors' calculation) (Moran et al., 2019). The paper's closing sentence, that the risk was about twice as high with amphetamine, rests on the crude shares of patients (0.21% against 0.10%), which do not allow for the longer time people who started amphetamine stayed in the study (median 155 against 113 days in one database and 162 against 123 in the other; from the printed counts and rates, about 83,700 against 59,600 person-years, editors' calculation): the two rates give a ratio of 1.59 (editors' calculation), and the hazard ratio is 1.65. The comparison is not randomized. People were matched on what the claims record (age, year, sex, region, insurance, markers of ADHD severity, other psychiatric diagnoses and medicines, recorded substance use disorders, type of prescriber and use of care; largest standardized difference 0.02); in the full unmatched cohort of 337,919 the hazard ratio was 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77) unadjusted and 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92) adjusted; two stricter definitions of psychosis gave 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) and 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22); emergency or inpatient care for alcohol, cannabis, opioid or other substance use disorders and for depression without psychosis, used as checks, did not differ between the groups (hazard ratios 0.91 to 1.12, all intervals including 1); and, by the authors' bias analysis, cannabis use would have had to be 97.0% among amphetamine starters, against an estimated 35.8% among people with ADHD, to explain the finding (assuming that any cannabis use doubles the risk of psychosis). Claims cannot show unrecorded drug use, early symptoms before psychosis, family history, the dose, or whether the medicines were taken; amphetamine was prescribed more to older patients and by family or internal medicine doctors (72.5% of their patients, against 51.6% of paediatricians'); and people who switched to the other stimulant (13.8% of methylphenidate starters, 5.6% of amphetamine starters) stopped being followed at the switch. Episodes in the first 7 days were not counted, and the median time to an episode was 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Psychosis counted only when coded and treated with an antipsychotic within 60 days (positive predictive value 91.3% in a review of records by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug, 93.1% in an outside validation), so milder or untreated symptoms are not counted. Results by age, by type of prescriber and by formulation were post hoc, with no test of whether subgroups differ. The people studied had commercial insurance; the authors say the results do not apply to people with public or no insurance, and the study says nothing about adults over 25, children under 13, use over years or use without a prescription. No other study on file measured psychosis with these medicines; the two network meta-analyses of trials did not study it. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 337,919 people aged 13 to 25 with an outpatient ADHD diagnosis in two US commercial insurance claims databases (Optum Clinformatics, IBM MarketScan) who newly started a prescribed stimulant between January 2004 and September 2015, without earlier psychosis, bipolar disorder or antipsychotic use; 221,846 after 1:1 propensity-score matching (mean age about 17; about 37% female)
lines.exposure: Starting amphetamine (amphetamine–dextroamphetamine, dextroamphetamine or lisdexamfetamine), as dispensed by an outpatient pharmacy; follow-up from day 7 after the first dispensing to 60 days after the end of supply, a switch to the other stimulant, psychosis or the end of data (dose not recorded)
lines.comparator: Starting methylphenidate (or dexmethylphenidate), matched 1:1 on a propensity score within each database
lines.outcome: A new psychotic episode: a new diagnosis code for psychosis with an antipsychotic prescription the same day or within 60 days (validated against records reviewed by a psychiatrist unaware of the drug), as incidence per 1,000 person-years and hazard ratio
lines.magnitude: Moran et al. (2019). Matched population (primary, prespecified): 221,846 people (110,923 per group), 143,286 person-years; 343 episodes (2.4 per 1000 person-years); methylphenidate 106 (0.10%), amphetamine 237 (0.21%); incidence 1.78 against 2.83 per 1000 person-years; pooled hazard ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.31 to 2.09). Editors' calculations: 343 of 221,846 = 1 in 647 (paper: approximately 1 in 660); rate ratio 2.83/1.78 = 1.59; rate difference 1.05 per 1000 person-years (paper: approximately 1); person-years implied by the printed counts and rates 106/1.78 = about 59,600 and 237/2.83 = about 83,700 (sum about 143,300; printed 143,286); crude ratio from the counts 237/106 = 2.2. Median follow-up: Optum 155 (IQR 82 to 318) against 113 (82 to 209) days; MarketScan 162 (82 to 339) against 123 (82 to 228). Median time to the episode 128 days (IQR 48 to 333). Full cohort (337,919: 119,708 and 218,211): 120 (0.10%) against 429 (0.20%); unadjusted HR 1.44 (1.17 to 1.77); adjusted 1.55 (1.25 to 1.92). Stricter definitions (matched): 89 (0.08%) against 211 (0.19%), HR 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), PPV 96.7%; 71 (0.06%) against 163 (0.15%), HR 1.68 (1.26 to 2.22), PPV 98.2%. Post hoc: 13 to 17 years 1.62 (1.24 to 2.12); 18 to 25 years 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00); family or internal medicine 1.78 (1.21 to 2.62); paediatricians 1.70 (1.09 to 2.67); psychiatrists 1.38 (0.93 to 2.04); extended-release only 1.77 (1.30 to 2.40); lisdexamfetamine against extended-release methylphenidate 1.54 (1.10 to 2.16); immediate-release 1.32 (0.77 to 2.29). Negative controls at 100 days: alcohol use disorder 1.12 (0.95 to 1.33), other substance use disorders 1.10 (0.95 to 1.29), cannabis 1.12 (0.91 to 1.38), opioids 0.91 (0.63 to 1.33), depression without psychotic features 1.03 (0.84 to 1.27). Bias analysis: cannabis use among amphetamine starters would need to be 97.0% (against 35.8%, relative risk 2.0 assumed). Switching: 16,489 of 119,708 (13.8%) and 12,233 of 218,211 (5.6%).
lines.reasoning: Observational (a claims cohort) starts low (METHODS §6.3); no domain downgraded and no upgrade (hazard ratio below 2; no dose data). Low for the statement as worded: in commercially insured US 13- to 25-year-olds starting a prescribed stimulant for ADHD, new psychosis treated with an antipsychotic was rare in the first months (about 1 in 650 people; 1.78 and 2.83 per 1,000 person-years) and occurred at a higher rate after starting amphetamine (hazard ratio 1.65; about 1 extra episode per 1,000 person-years). The paper's closing description of the risk as about twice as high is not used: it rests on crude shares inflated by longer follow-up after amphetamine. Status single study: no replication is among the papers on file, and the two network meta-analyses of trials read in this round did not study psychosis.

lines.q: Is psychosis more likely on Adderall than Ritalin?
lines.short: A bit, in one big US study. But it's rare either way. Each year, about 3 in 1,000 people on amphetamine (as in Adderall) had it, against 2 on methylphenidate.
lines.but: It's one study of insurance records, not a trial. Things the records missed, like drug use or early signs of illness, could explain part of it.
how: It used records of about 222,000 young people, aged 13 to 25, with ADHD and US insurance. They had started either medicine and were matched on what the records showed.
Over about 4 to 5 months, 343 had a new psychotic episode treated with antipsychotic medicine, about 1 in 650. Per 1,000 people a year, that's 1.8 on methylphenidate and 2.8 on amphetamine.
That's about 1.65 times the rate, or 1 extra case per 1,000 people a year. The paper's own summary, about twice the risk, leaves out that amphetamine starters were followed longer.

Counting psychosis more strictly gave similar results. Emergency or hospital care for alcohol or cannabis wasn't more common after amphetamine. Records can't show the dose, missed drug use, or if pills were taken.

lines.statement: In 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30; at most 20 lifetime uses of psychedelics or MDMA) who each took MDMA (100 mg) and LSD (100 µg) at the same time, compared with each drug alone and with a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a calm hospital room (study conditions), the combination raised blood pressure and heart rate more than LSD alone, to about the levels of MDMA alone, but not body temperature, did not significantly lower the unwanted effects people rated on LSD, made the effects last somewhat longer than LSD alone, raised LSD's blood levels, and lowered and delayed MDMA's peak (Straumann et al., 2023). Heart and blood pressure (average of each person's highest value, ± SEM): systolic 150 ± 2.9 mmHg with both drugs against 137 ± 2.7 with LSD alone (p < 0.001), 148 ± 2.9 with MDMA alone (not significantly different) and 124 ± 2.4 with the dummy; diastolic 90 against 85 (p < 0.05), 89 and 77; heart rate 100 ± 3.6 beats a minute against 92 ± 4.5 (p < 0.05), 95 and 77. Temperature: 37.5 ± 0.08 °C with both drugs against 37.4 ± 0.06 with LSD alone (not significantly different), 37.3 with MDMA alone (lower than with both drugs, p < 0.05) and 37.0 with the dummy. Unwanted effects: complaint scores in the first 12 hours were 15 (± 2.2) with both drugs and 15 (± 1.9) with LSD alone (8.6 with MDMA alone, 1.9 with the dummy), and from 12 to 24 hours 5.5 against 3.1 (not significantly different); ratings of a bad drug effect (14 against 18 out of 100) and of fear (8.2 against 13) did not differ significantly from LSD alone; headache, lack of energy, loss of appetite and dry mouth in the first 12 hours were reported about as often with either drug or both (headache by 16 or 17 of the 24); some complaints were reported by more people with both drugs than with LSD alone: trembling (14 against 5 of 24), restless legs (12 against 6), teeth grinding or jaw stiffness (14 against 11) and, from 12 to 24 hours, loss of appetite (12 against 4) (counts, not tested); no severe adverse event occurred. On nausea the paper's statements disagree, and its supplement settles how many people had it: on the complaint list, 14 of the 24 reported nausea in the first 12 hours with MDMA alone, 7 with LSD alone and 11 with both (4 with the dummy; no test of these counts), which fits the results text (more frequent with MDMA than with LSD) but not the discussion's statement that nausea was about as frequent with both drugs as with either alone; the rating scale, which measures how strong the nausea felt rather than how many people had it, ran the other way, with peaks of 7.9 out of 100 with MDMA against 25 with LSD and 21 with both. Late in the LSD response the authors note trend-level, non-significant signs of lower well-being and more depressed mood with both drugs in some people; these show only in a supplementary figure, without tests at those hours, and the highest mood ratings did not differ from LSD alone. Length: by each person's 'any drug effect' ratings over time (from and to 10% of that person's highest rating), the effects lasted on average 9.9 hours with both drugs against 8.4 with LSD alone (p < 0.05) and 4.3 with MDMA alone; the longest lasted 21 hours with both drugs, against 11 with LSD alone (ratings were taken up to 12 hours and again at 24 hours, so a time beyond 12 hours lies between those two ratings; editors' note). Blood levels: with MDMA, LSD's peak was 2.1 against 1.9 ng/mL (p < 0.05), its half-life 5.2 against 3.9 hours (p < 0.001) and its total exposure 19 against 14 ng·h/mL (p < 0.01; about a third more, editors' calculation); with LSD, MDMA's peak was 208 against 233 ng/mL (p < 0.001; about a tenth lower, editors' calculation) and came later, at 3.5 against 2.8 hours (p < 0.01), with total exposure unchanged; the paper's text and abstract mention only the change in LSD's levels. The authors attribute the higher LSD levels to MDMA blocking an enzyme that breaks down drugs (CYP2D6), which they inferred from other studies and did not measure. Their statement that they found no sign of greater serotonin toxicity rests on 24 healthy people given one pair of doses together in a calm room, which cannot show rare or setting-dependent harms; other doses, other timing, repeated doses, heat, dancing, alcohol or other drugs, and people with heart or psychiatric conditions or on interacting medicines were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25 to 54), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 12 had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before (1 to 13 times); excluded were more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted), a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder and interfering medicines; Basel
lines.exposure: MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules; analysed 25.40 mg each) and LSD base 100 µg (oral solution; analysed content 92.5 µg) taken at the same time, double-blind and double-dummy, in a calm hospital room with one investigator (study conditions)
lines.comparator: LSD 100 µg alone, MDMA 100 mg alone and placebo in the same people, at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order
lines.outcome: Peak blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours, self-rated bad drug effect, fear and nausea, and adverse events; blood levels of LSD and MDMA over 24 hours
lines.magnitude: Straumann et al. (2023), 24 people (Table 1, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA; F(3,69); Tukey tests): systolic 124 ± 2.4, 148 ± 2.9, 137 ± 2.7 and 150 ± 2.9 mmHg (combination against LSD p < 0.001, against MDMA not significant); diastolic 77 ± 1.7, 89 ± 1.4, 85 ± 1.8 and 90 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD p < 0.05); mean arterial 92, 107, 102 and 109 (combination against LSD p < 0.001); heart rate 77 ± 2.6, 95 ± 3.4, 92 ± 4.5 and 100 ± 3.6 bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.05, against MDMA not significant); rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385 and 14678 mmHg × bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.001); body temperature 37.0 ± 0.05, 37.3 ± 0.07, 37.4 ± 0.06 and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05; MDMA against LSD not significant); pupil size 6.0, 7.1, 7.0 and 7.2 mm (combination against LSD p < 0.05; n = 23). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) 1.9 ± 1.1, 8.6 ± 1.8, 15 ± 1.9 and 15 ± 2.2 (combination against LSD not significant); subacute (12–24 h) −0.2 ± 0.5, 2.5 ± 0.9, 3.1 ± 1.0 and 5.5 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05). Visual analogue peaks (% of maximum): bad drug effect 0.2, 6.4, 18 and 14 (combination against LSD not significant); fear 0.2, 2.3, 13 and 8.2 (not significant); nausea 1.0, 7.9, 25 and 21 (MDMA lower than LSD, p < 0.001, and than the combination, p < 0.05; LSD against combination not significant). Blood levels (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI; paired t-tests): LSD peak 1.9 (1.7–2.1) alone and 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL with MDMA (p < 0.05); half-life 3.9 (3.5–4.4) and 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (p < 0.001); AUC∞ 14 (12–17) and 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (p < 0.01); apparent clearance 6.9 and 5.3 L/h (p < 0.01); time to peak 1.6 h in both. MDMA peak 233 (215–252) alone and 208 (189–228) ng/mL with LSD (p < 0.001); time to peak 2.8 (2.5–3.2) and 3.5 (3.0–4.0) h (p < 0.01); half-life 8.3 and 8.2 h; AUC∞ 3083 and 3068 ng·h/mL (some MDMA-alone values from 23 people). Editors' calculation from the printed means: LSD AUC∞ about 36% higher, MDMA peak about 11% lower. No severe adverse events. Supplement (Tables S4–S6 and S8, pp. 14–15 and 17): complaint list, number of the 24 in the first 12 hours (placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA; Table S6; no tests): nausea 4, 14, 7 and 11 (12–24 h: 1, 2, 2 and 3); headache 11, 16, 17 and 16; lack of energy 3, 12, 12 and 15; loss of appetite 1, 13, 12 and 16 (12–24 h: 0, 3, 4 and 12); dry mouth 3, 12, 17 and 17; trembling 1, 15, 5 and 14; restlessness in legs 2, 9, 6 and 12; teeth grinding or jaw rigidity 1, 9, 11 and 14; heart palpitations 2, 9, 9 and 10. 'Any drug effect' over time (Table S5; mean ± SEM, range; MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA): duration 4.3 ± 0.4 (0.7–10), 8.4 ± 0.4 (5.1–11) and 9.9 ± 0.8 h (5.1–21), F(2,46) = 49, the combination longer than LSD alone (p < 0.05); time to offset 4.9 ± 0.4, 8.9 ± 0.4 and 10 ± 0.8 h (the combination not marked as different from LSD); onset 0.5, 0.4 and 0.4 h (F = 2.2, p = 0.117). Mood scale peaks, LSD against LSD + MDMA (Table S4): well-being 4.9 ± 1.0 against 4.4 ± 0.9, depression 1.6 ± 0.4 against 1.5 ± 0.3, anxiety 1.0 ± 0.3 against 1.1 ± 0.3, none significantly different; the late differences appear only in Fig. S3 (p. 6), without tests by time point. Guesses (Table S8; during the session at 2.5 h / 24 h after / at the end of the study, % of 24): placebo named correctly 96 / 96 / 100, MDMA 83 / 96 / 100, LSD 71 / 58 / 75, LSD + MDMA 37.5 / 46 / 75; the combination taken for LSD alone 50 / 46 / 25.
lines.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim gives how long the effects lasted, as measured, but leaves out how strong the good effects felt, and gives no timing or dosing advice. The online supplement, read in round pdf-2026-11-26, settles the nausea counts and adds the duration and complaint counts; it does not change the rating.

lines.q: What if I take LSD and MDMA at the same time?
lines.short: Blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone, and bad feelings weren't clearly eased. In a lab study of 24 people, top blood pressure was 13 points higher.
lines.but: Healthy people took one amount of each, in a calm hospital room. Nothing serious happened, but 24 people can't show rare dangers.
how: 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days, at least 10 days apart. They got LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which.

With both, top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone; heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was not clearly higher than on LSD alone.

Bad-feeling, fear and complaint scores were not clearly lower than on LSD alone, and more people had trembling, restless legs or teeth grinding. Nausea in the first 12 hours: 11 of 24 with both, 14 on MDMA alone, 7 on LSD alone, 4 on the dummy. Nobody had a serious problem.

The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later. The effects lasted about an hour and a half longer than on LSD alone, and the longest lasted 21 hours.

lines.statement: In people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl and who had taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, remembering severe withdrawal on taking it was common, and more common the shorter the shortest wait after fentanyl that people reported, in one self-report survey analysed without adjustment (Varshneya et al., 2022, read from the author manuscript). Of 1,679 people whose answers were collected at admission by an outcomes-tracking system, 1,163 (69.3%) reported fentanyl use; 421 of them had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl and 57 had done so only with a shortest wait of 1 month to 1 year. Of the 685 whose shortest wait was under 1 month, 250 (36.5%; 95% CI 33.0 to 40.2, editors' calculation) said their withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine after fentanyl had been severe, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl, 30 (15.0%) said severe. Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine was remembered by 152 of the 339 people whose shortest wait was under 24 hours (44.8%) and 55 of the 160 whose shortest wait was 24 to 48 hours (34.4%), and, by the editors' reconstruction from the printed odds ratios (checked against the bars of Figure 1), by 25 of 97 at 48 to 72 hours (25.8%), 13 of 52 at 72 hours to 1 week (25.0%) and 5 of 37 at 1 week to 1 month (13.5%): a gradual fall, with no clear cut-off. The abstract's 22.19% for 'those who waited less than 24 hours' is 152 out of all 685, not out of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours (editors' calculation). The paper's odds ratios for severe withdrawal (under 24 hours 5.20, 95% CI 1.98 to 13.68; 24 to 48 hours 3.35, 1.24 to 9.09; 48 to 72 hours 2.22, 0.78 to 6.33; 72 hours to 1 week 2.13, 0.69 to 6.62) are unadjusted and compare each group with a reference the paper does not name, which the editors' exact reproduction shows to be the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; the results call the odds ratios of about 2 at 48 hours to 1 week no increase, and the conclusion compares with everyone who waited more than 48 hours, which the model did not do. The answers were remembered when people entered treatment, about one or more unspecified occasions; the shortest wait ever was not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal; the survey did not record the dose, form, setting or supervision of the buprenorphine, or whether withdrawal had begun before it was taken; and a single rating cannot tell withdrawal that buprenorphine brought on from withdrawal it did not relieve (the authors explain severe withdrawal after methadone as too little opioid effect early in treatment). The survey period, response rate, full questionnaire and centres are not described, and the descriptive appendix was not on file. Among the 152 people who had taken both medicines after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) remembered severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US treatment centres using one outcomes-tracking system (survey period and centres not described) whose main drug was opioids and who said they had probably or definitely used fentanyl before treatment: 1,163 of 1,679 (mean age 30.8 years; 70.6% men; 80.4% White; 43.9% said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission); withdrawal ratings analysed for the 685 whose shortest wait after fentanyl before buprenorphine was under 1 month and for 200 who had taken methadone after fentanyl
lines.exposure: Taking buprenorphine after fentanyl (any product; the table note names seven brands, Suboxone among them), grouped by the shortest time people said they had ever waited after fentanyl: under 24 hours, 24 to 48 hours, 48 to 72 hours, 72 hours to 1 week, 1 week to 1 month; dose, form, setting and supervision not recorded
lines.comparator: Shorter against longer shortest waits (reference, by the editors' reproduction of the printed odds ratios: the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month); methadone taken after fentanyl (200 people; 199 in the odds model); no adjustment for anything
lines.outcome: Self-rated withdrawal symptoms on taking buprenorphine (or methadone) after fentanyl, remembered at treatment entry (none, mild, moderate or severe; one item, not a validated scale); the authors take severe withdrawal after buprenorphine as precipitated withdrawal
lines.magnitude: Varshneya et al. (2022), Table 1 and text. Fentanyl use reported by 1,163 of 1,679 (69.3%; probably 180, definitely 983). Shortest wait before buprenorphine (of 1,163): under 24 h 339 (29.1%), 24–48 h 160 (13.8%), 48–72 h 97 (8.3%), 72 h–1 week 52 (4.5%), 1 week–1 month 37 (3.2%), 1 month–1 year 57 (4.9%), never 421 (36.2%); methadone 135, 22, 21, 13, 8, 29 and 935. Withdrawal after buprenorphine (N = 685): severe 250 (36.5%; Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2, editors), moderate 136 (19.9%), mild 122 (17.8%), none 177 (25.8%); after methadone (N = 200): severe 30 (15.0%; 10.7–20.6), moderate 29 (14.5%), mild 44 (22.0%), none 97 (48.5%). Severe within each waiting group (editors' calculation; the last three counts reconstructed from the printed odds ratios, adding up to 250 and matching Figure 1): 152/339 = 44.8% (Wilson 39.6–50.2), 55/160 = 34.4% (27.5–42.0), 25/97 = 25.8% (18.1–35.3), 13/52 = 25.0% (15.2–38.2), 5/37 = 13.5% (5.9–28.0); methadone 23/135 = 17.0%, 2/22, 2/21, 1/13 and 2/8. As printed in the abstract and results: 22.19% (152/685) and 8.03% (55/685); methadone 11.56% (23/199) and 1.01% (2/199). Odds ratios for severe withdrawal, unadjusted, against the 1 week–1 month group (editors' reproduction): buprenorphine 5.202 (95% CI 1.979–13.675; p = 0.001), 3.352 (1.237–9.089; p = 0.017), 2.222 (0.780–6.329; p = 0.135), 2.133 (0.687–6.620; p = 0.190); methadone 0.616 (0.117–3.247), 0.300 (0.035–2.606), 0.316 (0.036–2.750), 0.250 (0.019–3.342). Both medicines (n = 152): severe after buprenorphine 69 (45.4%), after methadone 20 (13.2%). 483 of 1,163 (41.5%) knew someone who used fentanyl and had precipitated withdrawal after buprenorphine. Complete relief of withdrawal: 68 of 177 (38.4%) for buprenorphine and 43 of 97 (44.3%) for methadone, denominators equal to the numbers reporting no withdrawal symptoms (who was asked is not stated).
lines.reasoning: A cross-sectional self-report survey starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). Rated as worded: how often people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine following fentanyl, and its association with the shortest wait they reported. It cannot give the incidence of withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine, or show that waiting longer prevents it, and no gradient was used to upgrade (unadjusted, self-reported groups). Status: single study; the paper cites only case reports and anecdotal accounts as earlier evidence. The waiting times appear only as the survey's groups, never as advice.

lines.q: Can Suboxone put you in withdrawal if you use fentanyl?
lines.short: Many say so. In a US survey, 37 in 100 who took Suboxone's main drug after fentanyl remembered severe withdrawal. After methadone, 15 in 100 did.
lines.but: These are memories, not records. And the survey couldn't tell if Suboxone caused the withdrawal or just didn't ease it.
how: 1,163 people starting treatment at 49 US centres said they'd used fentanyl. 685 had taken buprenorphine, Suboxone's main drug, within a month after fentanyl. 250 of them remembered severe withdrawal.

The shorter the shortest wait they reported after fentanyl, the more often they remembered it: about 45 in 100 under a day, 34 in 100 at 1 to 2 days, about 25 in 100 at 2 days to a week, 14 in 100 at a week to a month. There was no clear cut-off.
The paper's summary says 22 in 100 for those who waited under a day. That's out of all 685 people. Out of the 339 who waited under a day, it's 45 in 100.
Nothing else that differed between people was taken into account. The dose, the form and who gave it weren't asked.

lines.statement: As described in one editorial, with figures second-hand and cases gathered without a search, deaths during opioid withdrawal have been reported, all of them in custody, but the evidence is insufficient to say how often withdrawal leads to death, whether such deaths are increasing, or what the risk is outside custody. The editorial, by three researchers in Sydney, says that opioid withdrawal is generally seen as a flu-like illness, subjectively severe but objectively mild, unlike alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, which it calls life-threatening, and that death is uncommon but does occur (Darke et al., 2017). Its proposed mechanism: persistent vomiting and diarrhoea, if untreated, can lead to dehydration, raised blood sodium (hypernatraemia) and resulting heart failure. Its cases: a woman in custody in the United Kingdom in 1998 who went into heroin withdrawal with persistent vomiting, sudden weight loss and dehydration and died of brain damage from lack of oxygen after a cardiac arrest, a death for which a failure of the duty of care was argued successfully before the European Court of Human Rights; and 10 deaths in United States jails between 2013 and 2016 that the authors were aware of (six women and four men, aged 18 to 49), which its appendix lists only by year of death (one each in 2013 and 2014, five in 2015, three in 2016), sex, age, place (seven states) and source: news or web reports for nine of them (two share one report) and, for one, a district attorney's letter on the investigation of the death, although the text describes all ten as reported in the press. The authors judge every such death preventable with appropriate medical care, say that in each case the process of dying appeared prolonged, with ample time to treat, and describe the deaths as neglect or a lack of medical resources, judgments that rest on the reports they cite rather than on case details they present; they cite one survey in which only a quarter of US jails had alcohol or drug detoxification services. The editorial gives no rate and no number of people going through withdrawal, and its statement that the number of withdrawal deaths in US jails is rising comes without counts over time; the cases come from news reports, a court case and a district attorney's letter, so deaths that were not reported, or not attributed to withdrawal, are missed, and neither the text nor its appendix describes the cases' causes of death beyond the UK case, their symptoms, how long they were ill, their medical histories, the care they received or other drugs involved, including withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.

lines.q: Can opioid withdrawal itself kill you?
lines.short: Deaths have been reported, but nobody knows how often. One editorial lists 11, all in jail. It suggests vomiting and diarrhoea, left untreated, can dry the body out until the heart fails.
lines.but: It's one editorial's short list, from the news, a court case and a prosecutor's letter. It has no medical details. And nobody counted how many went through withdrawal, so there's no rate.
how: The authors' idea: vomiting and diarrhoea that don't stop, left untreated, dry the body out. Blood sodium rises, and the heart can fail.

The cases: a woman in custody in the UK in 1998, and 10 people in US jails from 2013 to 2016, aged 18 to 49. For those 10, the list gives only the year, sex, age, place and a news source (for one, a prosecutor's letter).
The authors say each death came slowly, with time to treat it, and call the deaths neglect or a lack of medical care. Their list gives no medical details to check this.
They say such deaths are rising but give no counts over time. Nothing here covers withdrawal outside custody.
